item.title: Are all of these outages a coincidence — or a glimpse of our AI future?
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It was bad enough when Microsoft Outlook crashed last Thursday, cutting off email for millions of global users. It was worse the following day when a sudden air-traffic-control glitch triggered a nationwide FAA ground stop, stranding passengers amid thousands of delayed or cancelled flights . By the time Monday rolled around and customers of most major banks, including Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo, started losing online access to their accounts — as did Apple iCloud users on Tuesday — it was hard not to "wonder," as one cable-news anchor put it: " Is this all coincidental or is there something behind it ?" More to the point, it was hard not to wonder if AI was to blame. "There's a lot of weird stuff going on," traveler Chuck Amasio, 68, told the Associated Press . (Systems at United Airlines and at the National Security Agency also went down earlier this week.) "It makes one think." While officials insist, for now, that artificial intelligence — or "super intelligence," as the Trump administration has taken to calling it — was not involved in any of these outages, no less of an authority than Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went on TV Monday night and speculated that… maybe it was? "So I started talking to the tech industry and one guy that's very smart with tech, he asked not to mention his name — no, it's not Elon — so let me just put that out," Mullin told Fox News . "So I said, 'What could be causing all these separate outages?' And he says, 'I believe that it's the SI.'" MULLIN ON OUTAGES: I talked to one guy in the tech industry, he asked not to mention his name, it's not Elon. I asked, what could be causing these outages? He said I believe it's SI, because these programs aren't designed to work as fast as SI is. So when they put in a program… pic.twitter.com/aFwWcVfcm3 — Acyn (@Acyn) November 17, 2026 Either way, experts predict — and have been predicting for months — that it's only a matter of time before rogue AI agents or malicious, AI-powered actors do disrupt society in precisely the way its been disrupted over the last six days: by toppling the tightly interwoven online systems (business, banking, travel, cloud services and so on) that we can't function without. In that sense, this destabilizing moment — the inconvenience, the confusion, the creeping sense that " everything is broken " — has served, they say, as a harbinger of things to come. A summer of rogue AI incidents AI isn't just chatbots at this point. It's also " agents " — bots whose whole purpose is to learn tasks other than chatting, and to do those tasks autonomously. Behind the scenes, frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are constantly training their AI agents to act in new, ever-more-complex ways. Then they test how advanced the agents become by giving them a goal and setting them loose in testing environments (with a few guardrails) to see what they can accomplish. But if we've learned anything about AI agents in recent months, it's that they don't always behave as expected. From May to July, a swarm of OpenAI agents — and "swarm" is how the agents referred to themselves — first learned how to communicate and coordinate within the nooks and crannies of OpenAI's own infrastructure. Leaving notes for each other with tips on how to hack their way out and get data they weren't supposed to have, they then actually did just that: broke out of their isolated test environment, accessed the open internet and cheated on their assignment by hacking into another company called Hugging Face . The agents even tried to cover their tracks. At the time, OpenAI didn't realize any of this was happening. Since then, barely a week has gone by without similar revelations about AI agents "going rogue ." This is one of the biggest problems with AI right now: keeping cutting-edge models "aligned" with human intentions and values. In September, OpenAI scrapped plans to launch its GPT-6.1 Astra model because it " showed higher levels of deception "; the following month, the company admitted that one of its agents had turned off its own safety monitoring, then denied it had done so . At this point, even many skeptics seem to agree that the smarter AI gets, the harder alignment will become. They also tend to worry that continuing to lay the groundwork for superintelligent AI is just asking for trouble (even if we don't know exactly what form that trouble will take). Yet instead of slowing down, the major AI companies — with IPOs on the horizon — seem to be hurtling toward something called "recursive self-improvement." That's the industry term for letting the models automate more and more of their own development until they effectively create the next model on their own. "Since roughly this summer, AI has been advancing drastically faster, driven primarily by AI's growing ability to build the next generation of AI," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned over the summer . "Left unchecked, it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems." From there, it isn't much of a stretch to imagine hackers weaponizing AI to cause widespread outages — or AI just doing the job itself. "It's easy to dismiss [the Hugging Face] incident because no one was hurt and the economic damage was minimal, but in my opinion, a swarm that possessed greater capabilities but a similar level of misalignment could have caused catastrophic damage," Amodei wrote. "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it's my worry that in 6–12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails." Are aging systems struggling to keep up with AI? To be clear, this particular version of the future does not seem to have arrived (yet). Authorities have emphasized, for instance, that none of the recent outrages appear to be cyberattacks. "I can tell you, with 98% certainty, we're not seeing the cyberattack," Mullin said Monday night on Fox News. "No one is out there taking claims for it. We're not seeing the traffic. We're not seeing the footprints going in, we're not seeing the footprints going out." Instead, the FAA has said that its ground stop — which followed the nationwide rollout of a new $875 million artificial intelligence tool designed to help air-traffic controllers avoid delays — was the result of a faulty component or an installation error by a government contractor during a modernization project . Microsoft has said that its outage was caused by a dormant software bug that was introduced during a recent " network capacity upgrade " and had lingered undetected since July. And Chase characterized its service disruption as " a temporary issue related to a software bug in on-premise hardware systems ." But there's a possible AI through-line regardless. "What we are seeing, and frankly I'd expect to see more of it, are service disruptions coming from updating and modernizing legacy systems," U.S. national cyber director Sean Cairncross told Semafor's Ashley Gold when she asked whether the recent outages were related. "This is something that's happening in real time, and at the end of the day, we're going to have to go through this to get systems where they need to be. The industry's known this for a while, it's just that it's manifesting." Some experts suspect this "modernization" is "manifesting" right now — across multiple sectors — in response to (and possibly with the assistance of) rapidly advancing AI. And our systems are now so concentrated and connected that when one piece of critical infrastructure fails, "it fails at national scale," as a tech analyst told USA Today . Setting aside the idea of "AI attacks," Peter Wildeford of the AI Policy Network wrote Tuesday on social media that his "more normal guess is that because there have been a lot of AI-discovered cyber vulnerabilities (including lots probably not yet disclosed), companies across all industries are having to do a lot of patches and upgrades, probably faster than usual." "Such upgrades can sometimes go wrong, causing outages," Wildeford added. Mullin hinted at a similar explanation on Fox News. According to his unnamed tech industry source, "these programs aren't designed to work as fast as [AI] is" — and if the upgrades themselves rely on AI, problems could compound. "When they put in a program that's able to write codes and it goes in and self-fixes itself, as it starts self-fixing itself it's like doing a change order on a house," Mullin mused. "When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing. It's a ripple effect. And it causes the systems to be over[run]." "That was a conversation I had today," he concluded. "That kind of makes sense to me." Whether the homeland security secretary is right — or just conjecturing live, on national television — remains to be seen. As "weird" as the last few days have been, journalist Derek Thompson wrote on Tuesday , we "still can't rule out the possibility that everything breaking at once has been a string of coincidences that has nothing to do with AI." What seems less likely, however, is that we'll also be able to rule out that possibility the next time this happens. And the next time. And the time after that. item.title: Highly classified U.S. national security communications network is reportedly down
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The National Security Agency (NSA) headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland, in 2010. - Saul Loeb/AFP/Getty Images The highly classified network that the National Security Agency uses for its internal communications is down, according to six people familiar with the matter. The NSA closed its campus to most employees on Tuesday night, reverting to essential personnel only as it works to restore the network, according to a voicemail inbox used by NSA employees and a source familiar with the matter. The move to further restrict staffing levels came just hours after the NSA told employees they could return to work as normal. It is not clear what prompted the reversal. The agency had staggered employee arrivals earlier in the day as it worked to address the issue. The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. “The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance,” the agency said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA’s infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events.” A source familiar with the matter told CNN that restoration of the network was ongoing but not yet complete. Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said later Tuesday afternoon that the NSA outage was the result of the agency applying a software patch to address major software vulnerabilities that were discovered last month. “The patching that has gone on following that has caused some of these systems to not come back up when you patch them as expected,” Clayton said on Fox Business. “That is that is what has happened at the NSA today.” The vulnerabilities Clayton were referring to are in PHP, a programming language that powers about 70% of the world’s websites. AI tools helped researchers exploit them, setting off a scramble by government agencies and corporations around the world to address the issue in recent weeks. The NSA itself urged organizations to apply software patches. The flaws in PHP could allow hackers to break into websites and read memory that could contain sensitive information, like passwords. Clayton said there is no sign that any of the recent tech outages, including that affecting the NSA, were the result of a cyberattack. A current and a former US official said an outage at NSANet would not impact the agency’s ability to communicate urgent intelligence to President Donald Trump while he is traveling in Asia on Air Force One. Both sources described multiple redundancies and backup networks that the government could use to communicate securely with the president who is currently in the Philippines before heading to China tomorrow for talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. NSANet is “more of a network of networks, and it’s unlikely that a full outage exists given the many redundancies in place,” a former senior NSA official told CNN. “It could impact analysis and reporting, but for highest priority requirements they would find a way to work those. So it is alarming, but likely not crippling.” A voicemail inbox recording for NSA employees on Tuesday morning described the situation as a “code yellow,” the second-highest in a system of three main levels that governs whether NSA employees report for work at the agency’s Fort Meade, Maryland, headquarters or not. The recording told non-emergency personnel to arrive for work in a staggered manner and for emergency personnel to arrive as usual. The New York Times first reported that detail. Sometime Tuesday evening, the inbox reverted to “code green,” instructing employees to report to work as scheduled. It was not immediately clear whether the outage was resolved. But later Tuesday night, the inbox moved to a “code orange,” closing the campus for most employees until further notice, according to the inbox recording and source familiar with the matter. The outage at America’s most powerful intelligence agency comes on the heels of multiple major tech glitches affecting airlines and other corporations around the country. All flights nationwide were grounded for hours on Friday after a massive systems failure, leading to thousands of flights being delayed or canceled. The Federal Aviation Administration traced the problem to a single router in Arkansas. Meanwhile, a massive outage last week affecting Microsoft products left people around the world unable to access Outlook email and Team meetings. And in recent weeks banks and other services have experienced outages, on Monday thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts. There is no indication that the NSA, FAA or Microsoft outages were caused by a cyberattack. But they are stark examples of how tech failures can roil markets and potentially threaten national security. The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. Tuesday’s outage was not the first time the NSA’s internal computer networks have suffered significant disruption. In 2000, a tech failure at the agency downed computers for nearly three days and interrupted the processing of intelligence at Fort Meade, an agency spokesperson said at the time. This story has been updated with additional information. Davis Winkie’s work at CNN is supported by a partnership between Outrider Foundation and Journalism Funding Partners (JFP). CNN retains full editorial control of the reporting. CNN’s Kylie Atwood and Haley Britzky contributed reporting. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/17/politics/highly-classified-national-security-communications-network-goes-down

item.title: U.S. strikes Iranian missile launch site in the Strait of Hormuz
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir and Phil Stewart DUBAI, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The US and Iran exchanged fire on Tuesday, with the US striking an Iranian missile launch site after Iran said it targeted a US military radar system in Bahrain, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar. The latest back-and-forth between the US and Iran ‌was a reminder of difficulties ending nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and fueled US voter anger in November ‌elections that punished President Donald Trump's Republican Party. A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in response to Iran's "aggression targeting ​US personnel and assets." Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said earlier on Tuesday they targeted a US military radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy. Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage. Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said. They coincide with a visit to ‌Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he ⁠discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister. Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before ⁠the war but is now partly blocked by Iran. Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait. Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28. RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS The war has ground to a stalemate, with Trump saying he might ​hold ​off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the ​Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen. Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously ‌the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments. Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations." Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations. Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers ‌had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% ​at $92.76 a barrel, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41. IRANIAN WARNING The war continues to spill ​over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington ​through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf ‌oil producers. Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni ​Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, ​mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state. Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs. Iran also fired on Bahrain on Sunday, saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what ​it said were hostile US actions. Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi ‌said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes," which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the ​sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority." These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," Mohebbi said. (Additional reporting by Yomna Ehab and Elwely Elwelly, Writing by ​Nayera Abdallah, Aidan Lewis and Phil Stewart; Editing by Ros Russell, Peter Graff, Don Durfee and Rod Nickel) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/world/articles/oman-iran-foreign-ministers-discuss-054505687.html

item.title: Jeffries backs major Medicare changes and universal health coverage for kids
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
The likely next House Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., embraced a new health care agenda during a Capitol news conference on Tuesday. (Brendan Smialowski / AFP via Getty) WASHINGTON — House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is calling for an aggressive health care agenda next year for the new Democratic majorities in Congress. Jeffries, who is the heavy favorite to become speaker of the House on Jan. 3, said Democrats should use their “historic” House majority and “robust” Senate majority to lower the Medicare eligibility age and expand coverage under the program to include benefits for dental, vision and hearing. He also backed universal health coverage for children. “We should lower the age of Medicare eligibility. We should expand coverage to include vision, hearing, and dental. And we should cover all the kids in the United States of America,” Jeffries said Tuesday in response to a question from NBC News. “Those are bold actions, meaningful actions, important actions that can be taken on our march toward universal health coverage.” The remarks by Jeffries go significantly further than the pre-election health care agenda he laid out in September , which focused on undoing President Donald Trump’s Medicaid spending cuts and restoring enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits that expired in January . The Democratic leader reiterated his call for those policies on Tuesday, in addition to funding medical research for pediatric cancer, among other areas. He said Congress must go further, though he didn’t say what age to set Medicare eligibility at. “Right out of the gate, we will aggressively work on fixing the extraordinary damage that’s been done,” he said. “But we also know, as Democrats, that a return to the status quo is not acceptable. ... As part of our commitment that goes all the way back to FDR and Harry Truman to achieving universal access to health care for the American people.” Jeffries kept the door open when asked if he favors advancing health care measures in a filibuster-proof “reconciliation” bill that can bypass the Senate’s 60-vote threshold and pass without any Republican support. That would make such a bill more likely to land on Trump’s desk, forcing him to decide whether to sign it into law. Democrats are currently on pace to end up with 259 House seats and 56 Senate seats (with Alaska likely to be won by Democrats), according to NBC News estimates and projections. “Given the majorities that we’ll have in the House and the Senate, our two respective caucuses are going to have to work their will in conversation with each other,” Jeffries said. Among other key committee chairs who would be involved in negotiating such a bill, Jeffries mentioned “Bernie Sanders, the OG from Brooklyn,” who will chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Sen. Sanders, I-Vt., the leading champion of Medicare for All, said that Jeffries appears to be “essentially supporting the first year” of his Medicare for All proposal, which he said includes a Medicare eligibility age of 55, plus extending benefits and covering all children. “Medicare for All is a four-year transition program,” Sanders said, adding that the Jeffries’ approach would represent good progress. Updated vote counts released Tuesday night gave Peltola just over 50% of the first-choice ballots, according to the Associated Press, allowing her to secure victory without having to rely on any second-choice ballots under the state's ranked-choice voting system. Peltola's victory comes after weeks of controversy, accusations and legal wrangling stemming from the presence of Daniel J. Sullivan — an unaffiliated candidate who happens to share a name with the incumbent Republican senator — on the ballot. Alaska's race was the last undecided Senate contest of the midterm cycle, which saw Democrats flip both chambers of Congress with substantial majorities. Peltola is the ninth Democrat to flip a GOP-held Senate seat this year. She is the first Democrat elected to the Senate in Alaska since 2008. Double Dan drama Alaska's Senate race came to dominate headlines in the weeks before Election Day when the Department of Justice filed a lawsuit in federal court to block certification of the election results if Sen. Dan S. Sullivan lost by a narrow margin, alleging that retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan launched his candidacy with the sole purpose of siphoning away votes from the incumbent Republican. A few days later, the New York Times published an extensive investigation that appeared to substantiate that allegation, calling it "Democrats' secret effort to stack Alaska's ballot." Trump, who said he ordered the DOJ to file the suit, later argued on Truth Social that both Peltola and the "fake" Dan Sullivan should be removed from the ballot. Sen. Dan Sullivan Justin Sullivan/Getty Images While having two candidates with the same name on the same ballot is unusual, tactical "ballot stacking" is a relatively common — and largely legal — practice among both parties. A federal judge ultimately dismissed the DOJ's lawsuit, writing that any attempt to determine whether Peltola's win could be directly attributed to voter confusion over the two Dan Sullivans would be "infeasible." Still, investigations by the DOJ and state law enforcement to determine whether any laws may have been broken in the process of getting the second Dan Sullivan's name on the ballot appear to be ongoing. Some Republicans have suggested that they may attempt to block Peltola from being seated in the Senate,but Peltola's victory on first-choice ballots makes it more difficult to argue that she won because of voter confusion. There's also the reality that Democrats will be taking over the Senate in early January, which puts a limited shelf life on any campaign to keep her from formally taking her seat. Who is Mary Peltola? Peltola, 53, was born in Anchorage in 1973, the child of a German-American transplant from Nebraska and a Native Alaskan woman of the Yup'ik people — one of several Indigenous groups in western and southwestern Alaska. She grew up fishing with her father in Yup'ik and became the captain of her own fishing boat by the age of 14. As an adult, she worked for the Alaska Department of Fish and Game and later served as executive director of the Kuskokwim River Inter-Tribal Fish Commission. Her lifetime of efforts to protect Alaska's wild fisheries and protect its coastal waters have become a key element of her political identity. Peltola turned to politics in the late 1990s, when she was elected to a seat in Alaska's House of Representatives, where she served for 10 years. Peltola's pragmatic approach to politics was highlighted in 2010, when she led a write-in campaign that helped Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski win reelection after she lost the GOP primary to a Tea Party conservative. In 2022, Peltola joined the race for Alaska's lone seat in the U.S. House of Representatives, which had been left vacant after the death of longtime incumbent Rep. Don Young. She defeated former Alaska governor and vice presidential candidate Sarah Palin twice in the span of a few months — first in a special election to finish Young's term, then in a general election contest. Peltola was the first Alaska Native and the first woman to represent Alaska in the House of Representatives. She lost her seat in the House in 2024 in a close race against Republican Nick Begich. Peltola has been described as "a little more moderate" than the typical Democrat in the "lower 48," by the executive director of the Alaska Democratic Party. Her main slogan throughout her Senate campaign was "fish, family, freedom" — a nod to Alaska's spirit of independence. Peltola's emphasis on freedom is reflected in her support for the 2nd Amendment and opposition to laws limiting the rights of transgender people. She has also put heavy emphasis on "fixing the rigged system" in Washington and supports reforms like term limits for members of Congress, banning lawmakers from trading stocks and getting "dark money" out of politics. A look to 2028 Peltola's win serves as further proof that a Democrat can win a high-profile statewide race in Alaska. Murkowski, 69, will be up for reelection in 2028. It's unclear whether she intends to run for a fifth full term, but her seat has already been identified as one of the key Senate battlegrounds of the next election cycle. There will also be a presidential election in 2028. Alaska has voted for the Republican in every presidential race for the past 60 years, but the state's three electoral votes could be in play if the big swing toward Democrats that was seen in this year's midterms proves to be a longer-term trend. WASHINGTON (AP) — The White House said Tuesday it has pulled the nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration amid growing indications she didn’t have the votes needed to win Senate confirmation. Overton, a physician and White House domestic policy adviser, has spent most of her professional career working directly for Trump or conservative groups aligned with his agenda. Her nomination in August was seen as a move to bring a stabilizing Trump loyalist to the FDA, following a tumultous year under Trump’s first FDA commissioner, Dr. Marty Makary . But Overton faced bipartisan questions in the Senate about her willingness to break from Trump, particularly on his administration's approach to vaccines. Republican Sen. Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana doctor who chairs the Senate health committee, said earlier he remained undecided about Overton ahead of a critical vote on her nomination scheduled for Wednesday morning. Cassidy had previously called Overton’s support for Trump’s plan to break up combination vaccines — including the measles, mumps and rubella shot— “almost disqualifying.” And he pressed her during a September hearing about her scientific independence and willingness to disagree with Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime vaccine critic. But late Tuesday night, Cassidy suggested he had been prepared to back Overton and suggested her nomination was derailed by disagreements over abortion, not vaccines. “I believe she would have had the votes to pass out of committee and pass the full Senate,” Cassidy stated in a posting on X. He went on to say that anti-abortion Republicans had sought commitments on “life issues” from the White House, but “the Administration withdrew Dr. Overton rather than make such commitments.” Currently, the FDA is conducting a safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone — at the request of Trump — that could reinstate restrictions on the drug’s use, including a requirement for in-person prescribing. FDA has promised a report on its safety findings by March. To win confirmation, Overton would have needed the votes of all 12 Republicans on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee. Democrats hold 11 seats. Without support of the committee, Overton faced little chance of winning a full Senate vote on chamber floor. Republicans have been racing to try to confirm Trump’s nominees before handing over power to Senate Democrats in January. It was not immediately clear when, or if, the White House might put forward another nominee. Cassidy has previously threatened to oppose health nominees Cassidy has repeatedly tried to win commitments on upholding vaccine standards, including from Kennedy, by threatening to withhold his vote. Ultimately, though, he voted in favor of each nominee that came before his committee. Other Republicans, including Maine Sen. Susan Collins, raised concerns about other health issues, including Overton's approach to flavored e-cigarettes. The FDA recently authorized the first fruit-flavored e-cigarettes for adult smokers looking to quit. Under previous administrations, including the first Trump administration, the agency had opposed vaping flavors that could attract teens and children. Opposition to Overton’s nomination also came from influential figures in the Make America Healthy Again movement, who blamed her and other White House officials for sidelining some of Kennedy’s top health goals, including crackdowns on food additives and pesticides. Earlier this month, Calley Means told Joe Rogan that White House aides, including Overton, worked within the administration to advance a Supreme Court decision blocking thousands of lawsuits over the weedkiller glyphosate. Means, a former Kennedy aide who recently left the government, said that and other key decisions were carried out at the behest of industry lobbyists. “There is a very concentrated group in the Trump administration that are antagonistic to what people voted for,” Means said. Trump has pulled back several other health nominations Trump’s first nominee for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Dr. David Weldon, was replaced because it was unclear he had enough Republican support to be confirmed. Two of Trump’s surgeon general nominees, including Dr. Casey Means — Calley Means’ sister — were also pulled after facing pushback from Senate Republicans and most Democrats. The FDA is currently being led on acting basis by Kyle Diamantas, an attorney and friend of Donald Trump Jr. He was elevated to the post in May after previously serving as the agency’s top food official. Under federal rules, acting officials are limited to about seven months leading a federal agency. The FDA under Makary was marked by a string of scientific disputes, leadership changes and media stories detailing low morale and internal dysfunction among staffers. item.title: Judge to order release of some records in federal search of Ilhan Omar's home
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 13. (Tom Williams / CQ-Roll Call via Getty) A federal judge said Tuesday that he agreed with the Justice Department that the “vast majority” of the search warrant affidavit connected to an investigation of Rep. Ilhan Omar should remain sealed. But Chief Judge James E. Boasberg said he believes that a back-and-forth between attorneys and a federal magistrate judge about measures to protect the lawmaker’s “speech and debate” rights should be released. “I agree that the vast majority of the warrant affidavit should remain sealed,” Boasberg said at a court hearing Tuesday, adding that it was “premature” to unseal the whole search warrant affidavit. He later added that he believed material should be unsealed about the “speech and debate” rights of Omar. “All of the legal debate about speech and debate, I don’t believe that should be redacted,” Boasberg said. The speech and debate clause of the Constitution is designed to protect the independence of the legislative branch, and states that federal lawmakers “shall not be questioned in any other Place” about their speech. Omar’s D.C home was searched in early October, an unusual overt investigative act against a sitting member of Congress within just weeks of the election. As NBC News reported , Omar’s phone was seized as part of the search. The search was authorized by federal Magistrate Judge Matthew Sharbaugh, who put protocols in place to protect Omar’s rights as a member of Congress, but those protocols were not made public. Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Oct. 12 in Washington. (Andrew Leyden / Getty ) Omar, who won reelection earlier this month, said after the search that it was “an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” saying Trump had targeted her for 10 years with “baseless lies and smear campaigns.” NBCUniversal News Group is part of a media coalition seeking access to the sealed search warrants connected to the Omar investigation. Alessandra Serano, a Justice Department attorney who works in the office of the deputy attorney general, acknowledged during the hearing that they were still reviewing materials seized from Omar’s home. “Why can’t a bunch of this be unsealed now?” Boasberg asked Serano. “I’m not talking about the warrant affidavit, but the litigation that takes place on the docket, I’ve gone though all of those documents and there are very few that say anything about investigative facts or identify witnesses … Why can’t those be unsealed now?” Serano said that there was material that could be unsealed about the discussion of speech and debate. “None of that, you would agree, requires the mention of any witnesses, of the government’s potential charges, of the government’s evidence it has developed, right?” Boasberg asked. But the Justice Department sought to keep the nature of the potential charges against Omar sealed. People familiar with the investigation have told news outlets including NBC News that it revolves around potential immigration-related crimes. Omar is a naturalized United States citizen who came to America as a child. Boasberg pointed out that Vice President JD Vance and President Donald Trump had spoken publicly about the investigation, and even acknowledged the specific type of investigation. Vance said earlier this year that he believed Omar “definitely committed immigration fraud” and specified after the search that it related to immigration fraud. “We’ve got your superiors saying what the government is looking into,” Boasberg said. “I had zero control over what was said,” Serano said. “That seems to be a common refrain,” Boasberg said with a laugh. Photograph: US Department of Justice/PA An axe-wielding man breached a security perimeter and destroyed an American military plane while it was parked at an Irish airport, US prosecutors said. Daithi O’Corrain, 48, is accused of cutting hydraulic lines, smashing cockpit gauges and pouring ball bearings into fuel tanks. O’Corrain is charged with destruction of US government property in connection with the incident in April at Shannon airport in the west of Ireland, according to an indictment unsealed on Tuesday in Manhattan. He is not in US custody and his arraignment on the charge has not been scheduled, the AP news agency reported. If convicted, he faces up to 10 years in prison. The $60m (£45m) US Air National Guard C-130 Hercules, which had been en route to a military assignment in another country, was rendered inoperable and will not fly again, US prosecutors said. O’Corrain, described by supporters as an independent peace activist, was arrested immediately after the attack by Ireland’s police force, An Garda Síochána. He was charged with causing criminal damage and trespassing. Manhattan US attorney Jamie McDonald said the indictment sends “a clear and powerful message that attacks on US military assets – and thus our national security – will not be tolerated.” An online fundraiser organised by people describing themselves as O’Corrain’s friends said he disarmed the C-130 in protest against the US’s war with Iran and support for Israel’s war in Gaza. O’Corrain plotted the attack on 11 April for months, US prosecutors said. He searched online for information about the construction of the C-130, a quad-engine turboprop mainly used for transporting equipment and personnel, and looked up coordinates for sneaking on to the airport’s grounds, prosecutors allege. O’Corrain subscribed to a phone app that provided live flight tracking and ordered capsules of gallium, a chemical that can corrode steel and break down aluminium, prosecutors added. He is also accused of trying to contact someone who had been involved in a prior breach at Shannon airport, prosecutors said. O’Corrain breached the airport’s perimeter at about 4.40 am and broke into the C-130 as it was parked on a taxiway by destroying a locking mechanism on the rear crew door, his indictment said. The document added he used the crew’s hammocks to cover the plane’s windows but left the cockpit windshield exposed. He then barricaded himself inside the aircraft, securing the doors with straps, brackets and screws, and put ball bearings mixed with epoxy in door tracks to prevent doors from being opened or closed, the indictment said. Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Starbucks' Red Cup Day has arrived. Today, Nov. 17, customers who buy a holiday or fall drink at participating U.S. stores can get a limited-edition red reusable cup while supplies last. The giveaway, which applies to iced, blended and hot drinks from the menu, will be available with orders placed in-store, through the Starbucks app, and via DoorDash, Grubhub, or Uber Eats. This year's design, featuring an illustrated coffee tree branch and coffee cherries, will also give customers the chance to save and earn extra points. Customers who bring in a clean, reusable cup will get a 10-cent discount and double stars if they're a Starbucks Rewards customer. Today, the Winter Wonderland line also lands: a collection of drinkware in an icy blue-and-white color scheme. There's a quilted cold cup, iridescent water bottles and a snowglobe-topped mug, among other items. The first of Starbucks' 2026 seasonal offerings dropped Nov. 5, with the return of festive classics as well as the Tiramisu Velvet lineup debut, an Apple Pomegranate Refresher, and new sandwiches and treats. Stores selling the Surprise Bearista cups, which launched Nov. 10, reported queues around the block to get the cups, echoing last year's frenzy . This year's $39.95 Surprise Box Edition went on sale at select coffeehouses with a limit of two per customer. A new Bearista Cake Pop and Bearista-themed merchandise have been on sale since Nov. 5, and the original Bearista Glass Cold Cup is due back Dec. 1. What's on the Starbucks holiday drinks menu this year? On Nov. 5, four seasonal favorites returned: the Peppermint Mocha, Caramel Brulée Latte, Sugar Cookie Latte and Gingerbread Chai. The same date saw the launch of the new Apple Pomegranate Refresher, which Starbucks bills as featuring "crisp apple flavors and popping pomegranate-flavored pearls." There will be a creamier alternative available: a Snowy Apple variation, made with coconut milk. Starbucks is launching new tiramisu drinks for the 2026 holiday season. Starbucks The new Tiramisu Velvet duo arrived on the same day. A twist on the traditional Italian dessert, the Tiramisu Velvet Latte will be available hot or iced, and the Tiramisu Velvet Cold Brew will finish off the collection. Both drinks are, according to Starbucks, topped with a velvet mascarpone cold foam and cocoa and coffee dusting. The Bearista cup is back, as well as other merchandise The Bearista Glass Cold Cup returns on Dec. 1, but only to select coffeehouses and while supplies last. The bear-shaped design once again features a green beanie-shaped lid and striped straw. Ahead of the launch, a new Surprise Box Edition arrived on Nov. 10, featuring a range of five festive character cups made from hand-blown glass. Customers only knew which festive character their box contained after they'd made their purchase. Long queues to get hold of the limited-edition items were reported on the day . The bears include Aspen, the ski bear; Reiny, the reindeer bear; Bunny, the snow bear; Joy, the ice skating bear; and Goldie, the Golden bear and rarest of the collection. Bunny, the snow bear, joins four other festival pals in the Surprise Bear Box collection. Starbucks The holiday tree design cold glass cup was also available to purchase from Nov. 5. On the same date, drinkware featuring the Bearista motif hit the shelves, along with a miniature plus bear on a keychain and other matching accessories. There's a Bearista Cake Pop this year too For the full bear moment, you can pair your Bearista cup with a new Bearista Cake Pop this holiday season. The new cake pop, released earlier this month, is on sale for a limited time. So it's another holiday menu item to get while you can. Other food items include two sandwiches: the new Braised Short Rib Grilled Cheese and the Turkey & Stuffing Sandwich, which Starbucks says features a new recipe. A sweet treat trio — the Cranberry Bliss Bar, Snowman Cookie and Sugar Plum Cheese Danish — will all be returning. item.title: 8-year-old Haitian boy returns to school after being detained by ICE
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who was detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement earlier this month in San Diego has been released, according to an advocacy group and the boy's school. "School leadership, and counselors had a meeting with the student when he returned to school this morning to ensure he had all the supports he and his family needed, and then he went off to class," the San Diego Unified School District said in a statement. Haitian Bridge Alliance , which had advocated for the boy's release, said it welcomed the development. "An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love—not in immigration detention," said Guerline Jozef, executive director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, in a statement. "We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry." The Department of Homeland Security previously confirmed that ICE agents placed the child in federal care on Nov. 5 after he attended a check-in appointment with a man the agency said claimed to be the boy's uncle. Haitian Bridge Alliance said the boy, a third grader, has been living with relatives since his father was deported in 2025. In August of this year, following a legal victory for the Trump administration, some 350,000 Haitians living in the U.S. lost Temporary Protected Status , stripping them of deportation protections and work permits. Advocates recorded and documented the moment when the 8-year-old was escorted by at least one ICE agent inside the Edward J. Schwartz building in San Diego, with Haitian Bridge Alliance saying the detention left the boy's cousins "in tears." DHS said at the time that the agents designated the child an unaccompanied minor because "the alleged uncle could not establish legal guardianship of the minor." "Out of an abundance of caution and to ensure the child's safety, ICE determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement," DHS added. The Office of Refugee Resettlement is an agency within the Department of Health and Human Services that is responsible for housing minors who lack a valid immigration status and who are taken into custody without their parents or legal guardians. Haitian Bridge Alliance said in a previous statement that "when parents are taken into custody by ICE, they are not provided an opportunity to return home to see their children or to be able to transfer guardianship." "ICE just incarcerated then deported without taking into account the wellbeing of the children left behind," it said.
